items.text: I agree with Misti Y-- that some people may love the Cirque shows and still dislike Le Reve. But that comparison is a separate discussion. For me, the theater and visual design are the best parts. The scenery and decor are breathtaking start to finish, and the whole concept behind the show is beautiful and appealing. Unfortunately, it doesn’t translate very well to the live performance. The storyline isn’t especially entertaining, and when I attended one performance, the stage malfunctioned repeatedly throughout the evening. That made it hard to stay engaged even during the more impressive scenes. Le Reve seems to be reaching for the flair and spectacle associated with Cirque, but it never quite gets there. I’d consider it mainly for the chance to experience that beautiful theater. Otherwise, you might be better off spending your money on another show.

I paid 38$ for this used mechanical keyboard. I think I got around 38$ worth of keyboard, probably a little more. The space bar rattles. Every time I hit it with my thumb its this hollow clatter sound, like a tray of cutlery being pushed around. I tune it out during the day but after midnight I start typing around it. The E key also repeats every now and then so it makes meeting into meeeting. Happens like once every few paragraphs, its rare enough to forget but common enough that I have to reread everything before I hit send. I messaged the seller to ask what switches it has but I was tired of waiting and bought it anyway. Answer came a week later after it was already on my desk. Brown switches for the record.

I keep it because its comfortable. Every key has a little bump partway down so my fingers know its registered without slamming to bottom. I can do long emails and my wrists are fine after. This never worked with my laptop and its flat keys. I thought about returning it. Return shipping would eat a good chunk of what I paid and I would be back on laptop. So its staying. Rattle and all.

saw this circus thing in Vegas. good show, I'd recommend it, but I'm knocking off a star. Hard to follow the storyline. Some of the songs are sleepy or just don't fit the action. Performers though are incredible, the athleticism and aerobic skill is impressive. The women are super freaky, they stay underwater for minutes.
The theatre is circular and so is the stage. Good view from every seat. There's three main stage entrances and they matter a lot for transitions. The stage and lights and setting are beautiful, real memorable atmosphere.
Tickets are reasonably priced compared to O and Love. I wanted more fireworks and fire but that's not a big deal. Storytelling and music need work but it's a good time and very visually striking.

I think remote work is being oversold as this all fixer. Two years mentoring five juniors and for someone still learning to code, it's really overblown. What jrs actually need is to sit in on design conversations, see how others debug, ask questions before spending hours confused. That stuff happens naturally in an office. Remote, they have to know when to cut in, set up a call, explain a problem they don't even fully understand. That's a tough skill to have before you've got a chance to learn it.

I've seen the feedback issues. A short comment on code review reads like the final word, not a learning opportunity. It takes longer, less momentum. The jrs I mentored improved faster with in-person pairing, whiteboard sessions, easy access to seniors.

I'm not pushing for offices or anti-flexibility. For self-driven devs it can be great. But for jrs, proximity gives you confidence, context, instincts. Sending them off with a laptop and a calendar is a drag on their development. And that means less good technical leadership down the line.

The mixer just kept humming, that low drone went through my boots every shift. Flour dust is everywhere, catches the fluorescent light like snow, its 3:17am. The sourdough loaves were resting on boards, crusts still pale and soft before final bake. Wiped my hands on my apron, was stiff with dried dough and sweat. Then I went to the front counter to check the lock, not because I needed to really, just paranoia.

And there it sat. The History of Salt. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had appeared every Thursday for six weeks now. Always on the glass display case, right beside the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp or anything. The bakery is not a branch of the municipal system. Picked it up, the cover felt cold. Opened it expecting blank pages or a forgotten bookmark, but instead a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, tapped down on the counter.

Unfolded it. Jagged handwriting, pressed hard into the fiber. It read "You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension." I stared at it. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. Looked at my own hands, red knuckled, dusted white. Closed the book, put it back on the glass, aligned the spine perfectly with the edge. Then turned off the overhead light above the display, so the book was in shadow.

I think Apple should be mentioned here. I used it at school. The school only let you have Apples, even though they cost about double the price of PC. We had it for middle and high school. The computers broke every month. Mine never once fell on the floor, but I replaced the hard drive 5 times in 4 years. Reinstalled the OS many times. A friend's MacBook Pro actually caught fire once, while he was watching a movie. Smoke alarm went off, very extreme. Support didn't diagnose the problem for us, they just back up the computer, wipe it, and restore the files. My criticism also applies to iPhones. I had the first iPhone and it was broken a lot. They seem to release a new iphone every 2 months, and the only improvement is the camera, slightly better. I will say one positive but with a qualifier: iPads are best tablets right now. But maybe android will catch up.

It's fine but not something I would build a trip around. Vegas isn't an attraction, but I've been there constantly since I was a kid so I've seen a ton of shows before I was 21, so I know what these can be.

The circular stage is actually good. From basically any seat you get a decent view. That's rare. Good news is if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, tickets are $99 instead of the usual $125. That helps.

Some individual acts are good. Performers are strong as hell, aerialists acrobats and stuff. But a lot of the feats feel like I've seen the same things done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows.

The story is the bigger problem. It's unclear, weak, or basically nonexistent. I left without knowing what it was trying to say. And too much going on at once. Too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many wow attempts. More restrained would hit harder.

Except for a few cool stunts it felt average. I wasn't blown away. No one I was with seemed overwhelmed either. A few friends did enjoy it. So if you've never seen it maybe check it out, especially with that deal. But I wouldn't see it again or pay full price a second time. It's the stereotypical huge flashy Vegas spectacle where more is better. More was messier for me.

Bought this mechanical keyboard second hand for 38 bucks and it’s been chaotic but surprisingly decent. Seller communication was atrocious. I asked them what switch type before I bought, they took a week to reply with one word. By then I had gambled and ordered it.

Board condition is well loved. Space bar rattles insanely badly, like a loose Lego brick. The E key randomly repeats. I type "theee" instead of "the" now and then, hilarious.

But here’s the twist. I love typing on it. Tactile feedback is fantastic. Very comfortable for pounding out long agonizing work emails. I considered shipping it back. But returning a 38 dollar slab of plastic heavy thing is more hassle than worth. I decided to keep it and I’ve grown fond of the flaws. If you don’t mind a bit of DIY tuning and a double-typing letter now and then, it’s a budget win.

float valve, float and valve. when water drops, the float sinks, opens valve, water comes in. and then it closes the valve, water goes up, float goes up, valve closes. at set level it shuts off, done. i've seen a lot of overflows, its just debris or build up, the valve doesn't close properly. or its set too high, its only closing when the trough is already overflowing.

a siphon moves water from one container to another over a high barrier. it works on gravity and atmospheric pressure. you fill the tube with water first, so it's just a solid column. then gravity pulls the water down the longer leg into the lower container. that pulls air pressure lower at the top. then air pressure on the water surface of the source pushes water up the shorter leg to fill that low pressure. That's what keeps it flowing.

you need the outlet lower than the source water surface. gravity is the driving force and it's really just the weight difference between the two columns. if the outlet is higher or level it won't work. it has to be lower. the descending column has to be heavier than the ascending one. If it's not, the siphon dies. air is bad. it breaks the water column. water molecules stick together to transmit the pull. when air gets in it breaks the chain. it equalizes the pressure inside with outside air. So the pressure diff that drives it is gone. siphon fails. You have to fill it with water again to get it working.

I found the sourdough on its second rise, again. Its always Thursday, always on the flour bin, always a copy of The Count of Monte Cristo with a Richmond Public Library stamp. Don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing, but at 3am my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. Anyway. This time a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. I wiped my hands on my apron leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, pulled it out. It said Page 142, please. I think they're watching the drop box now. In frantic spiky handwriting. Cold draft came through the kitchen, smelled like wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows but only saw my own tired reflection. I didn't open the book, carefully tucked the note back between the pages and slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, folded top down twice to seal it.

I considered shipping it back but the hassle was not worth it. So it stays on my desk, rattling, repeating. It is quietly earning its keep. Three stars.

Le Reve. Unbiased 4 stars, but for me its 2.5. I never wanted to see Cirque du Soleil before so this was my first show. I expected a ton of backflips and extreme acrobatics but it had far less of that, and way more interpretive dancing than I thought. Old school registers are really useful for historians. They help you piece together what the official story misses. You can see which kids came in, how regular they were and sometimes why they didn't come. So you figure out things like seasonal work, illness, weather, money problems, family stuff, migration or local emergencies. Also see differences between boys girls, ages, neighborhoods or social class. It shows how schooling fit into work and home routines. Look at enough years and you can see how habits and health changed. The problem is registers only say what the school wanted to write down. They don't really explain the kids experience. Absences might be wrong or missing or the teacher just guessed. So you really have to use them with other sources.

It’s my bakery. Mara finds the library book every Thursday morning, 2:17, on the back step of the bakery. It’s always the same book, A Field Guide to North American Moths. There’s a county library sticker on the spine, ghost pale, and there’s a little flour worked into the jacket, as if it was helping. She returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. By the third week she kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight it’s raining. The rain ticks against the alley door. The ovens breathe. Mara was shaping croissants, pressing butter into the dough with her palms, when the latch gives a tiny, guilty click. No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone, on the wet concrete. She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A slip of paper was folded once, between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea.” Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs. She looked at the alley, dented milk crates, steam off the drains. The city felt enormous for a second, then it didn’t. She tore a corner from an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05. Then she put the note inside the book, set it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

So our class built these bridges out of cardboard. Short beam stuff, arch inspired, triangular folds. Same cardboard, tried to keep the lengths and widths similar. We put them across two supports and added weights slowly just to see when they bend or tip or fall apart. Obviously it was all handmade and only a few trials plus its just a classroom, so dont think this is actual engineering data. The triangular ones held the weight better steady than the others. So the shape of the folds matters for how stable they are, but its really just a model activity.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. A Field Guide to Coastal Birds. The Harbor Street branch stamp on the inside cover said due date was March. Mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago but the delivery hatch beside it, the one the flour man used, never latched properly. Eleven Thursdays she had asked the day staff and checked the hatch for scratches and once she stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four and she was always at the ovens, her back to the door, when it did. Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. The ink was blotchy where someone pressed too hard. The note said I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want. She smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it was, because the pages did. Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll. She tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

I live in Toronto now. I dont use Hydro Ottawa anymore but i want to warn other customers about their billing practices its really alarming. I had an account for a year when i was renting a downtown apartment. I moved in with my parents to do my MA, cancelled the account and paid all outstanding charges. But they kept taking payments from my other bank account at random times for over a year. I called customer service repeatedly and sent them proof of the withdrawals. Reps kept saying the account was closed and no debits were happening. The truth came out when my parents and i cross checked our utility bills. Hydro had linked my banking details to my parents billing number because i mentioned moving home. Parents didnt notice since they got overpayment refunds all the time so credits looked normal. Spent hours on the phone with multiple reps. A manager finally investigated and confirmed the error and fixed it. They initially refused a refund and only offered an apology. Scared of automatic debit ever again. How they handle personal data and billing is really reckless and should concern everyone.

3:40am. Second batch of rye proofing. Marisol finds the book again. A library book on the flour bin by the back door, plastic jacket cold from the alley. Fourth Thursday in a row. Same book, A Field Guide to Night Birds, stamped Eastgate Branch, three weeks overdue. She's been carrying it to the drop box every Thursday on the walk home, but every Thursday it comes back. Feels like the building itself is borrowing it.

Wiped hands on apron, opened it. Folded index card falls out of the barn owl page.

It says you leave the vent fan on, alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. Signed R.

Read it twice, oven timer counting down. Outside the fan hummed, pushing warm air into dark. Turned card over, grabbed the grease pencil she uses to mark trays. Wrote "Rye's out at 4:15." Tore a heel off yesterday's loaf, wrapped in wax paper, put the book on top and propped back door open one inch.

So I did and came back and they were like no idea what I’m on about. Brilliant, £20 gone and I was fuming. Then at the gate they charged me £5 because I had water in my hand luggage even though I bought it inside the airport. Ryanair stopped flying from Liverpool John Lennon to Stockholm Skavsta so I fly Norwegian now. Norwegian’s service is poor too ironically but at least their planes feel newer and less outdated than Ryanair’s.

I got a real soaking on Tuesday, and by Thursday half my Brandywines had let go. You can see the seam running down the side of the fruit. It's just that old story of a dry spell followed by a sudden deluge. The inside takes water in faster than the skin can stretch to keep up. Sungolds are mostly holding out so far but I have a few that look like they might follow. Once it's happened you can't really get around it. The only thing that helps a bit is keeping that two day schedule on a more even footing, but in the end it doesn't matter much once the sky decides to let it all out at once. You'll likely get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use.

It's a lot more of a headache with Brandywines. That thick skin they have is a real liability in a storm like this. You might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting so much water in a single go.

College Board's hypocrisy is out of this world. A friend took a one hour sat subject test, but proctor in her room gave the room twenty minutes extra. She is a person who values integrity and knows this unfair advantage means the test was not standardised and so she reported through the official hotline to help avoid future misconduct. What happens? Total injustice by the institution. After an investigation, they claim there is insufficient evidence of misconduct to hold the proctor or the other students accountable. But absurdly, they claim there is enough evidence of misconduct by her and cancel her scores. So they punish the honest whistleblower and let the actual violation go. That's just so unfair and broken.

Its always the same book, a field guide to north american moths, elmwood branch, and the due date is stamped so far back that the ink is violet. I never see the person who leaves it. Thursdays it turns up behind the flour bins by the back door not the counter. So whoever leaves it knows i wont trip over it. My sourdough starter is my friend and i talk to it. Its friday morning and its gone and then thursday its back again. People are strange. I am elbow deep in rye dough by 2pm and at that hour i probably wouldnt notice a marching band. But i always see the book. First few weeks i just put it on the shelf by the register. Tonight there is a note tucked at page 114 about the luna moths. They only live a week and dont even eat. I keep thinking its a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before its gone? No signature, just pencil, pressed hard. I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then i pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling and wrapped it in brown paper and put it behind the flour bins.

My room can feel super stuffy even at like 72 degrees. The air is humid and it's heavy and I can't sweat so the heat just sticks to me. If you can't move the air around you get that stale air feeling. CO2 and odors and heat just hang around the people. Ventilation is a real thing. Air con cooling the air doesn't take the moisture out or air it out, it just cools. If you open a window and put a fan on it feels better, like a more fresh feeling.

I have mentored five junior engineers for the last two years and all of this stuff about remote work being a win for everybody isn't true for them. They don't need tickets or docs or scheduled meetings. What they need is to get into design arguments, to watch someone else get through a nasty bug, to get answers before a little uncertainty snowballs. You get all of that for free in an office. Remote means they have to figure out when to interrupt someone, get a call set up, and explain a problem they probably don't understand yet. That's pretty steep to ask of someone who hasn't had the chance to learn it.

I've watched this setup screw up feedback. A short note on a code review reads like a final judgment. The lag in getting answers kills forward motion. The people I worked with moved ahead a lot quicker in person, pairing up, whiteboard stuff, actually getting hold of the seniors. None of this means scrap flexibility, it works fine for people who can direct their own efforts. For a beginner, being around other people is what gets them there, it's how they pick up the confidence, context, judgment they're going to need. If you just hand a newcomer a laptop and a calendar and leave them to it, you are going to end up with weaker technical leadership down the road.

So a rain gauge is really simple. There is an opening of known area and it collects the rain and then reports it as a depth, in mm or inches. What that depth is telling you is if no water was lost to the ground or evaporation, this is how high it would have been. So you just measure the depth. Many gauges use a funnel, wide opening, that feeds into a narrow tube. Why do they do that? Because if the same volume of water goes into a narrow tube, it goes higher. So for small amounts of rain you can read it accurately. The scale on the tube is marked to account for the area ratio, so the readings are correct. A lot of error comes from wind. Wind picks up raindrops and blows them past the gauge, so you get undercounting. Also evaporation, splashing before you read it, can make the results off.

purchased used for 38 which was fair price as soon as I got it out of box. Had some dust between keys and a few shiny spots on caps, nothing worse than I expected from a used board.

The good part is it's really comfy, I type long emails for work and my hands feel less cramped than on my flat office keyboard. Switches are steady feel, not too heavy, case doesn't slide around my desk.

Issues are: spacebar rattles every time I hit it, loud enough to notice during quiet mornings. The 'e' key sometimes repeats so I type words like "neeed" when I go too fast. It's not constant, just happens enough that I proofread more.

Also I asked seller what switches it was, they responded a week later. After the keyboard had already arrived. Not great.

I'm keeping it, it's 38 dollars. Shipping back seemed more effort than it's worth.

went to this buffet on a friday around 4:30 pm and there was no line at all. two people cost about $130 so it was pretty steep. the seafood station had alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of vegas buffets but I hadnt run into rock crab claws anywhere else so those were interesting. the problem was there were no crab claw crackers. staff said wooden mallets were available but our table was so close to the next table that I didnt want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. so I just ate the crab legs.

the asian station didnt seem especially distinctive either. it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. dessert had gelato and various pastries but nothing really stood out. they also had fresh juices although I didnt try any.

overall I'd call the buffet acceptable but overpriced for what it offers. if you're curious its worth trying once especially if there's no wait but if the line is long I'd probably reconsider.

I think attendance registers are really useful to us. They're great primary sources. You can see how life actually was, what was going on. A sudden dip in attendance could mean the flu was bad, or harvest season, where they needed children to help on the farm. It shows the tension between education and work.
The registers are also a good source of info on class differences, or groups that don't come to school often.
But you have to watch out with them. Sometimes they're not always accurate. School headmasters were able to manipulate numbers to get funding, or avoid being scrutinised.
Also, they don't say why they didn't show up. So you have to go to other sources to find out why they didn't. But overall I think they're really useful for understanding the community and how it worked, and how it was, and what was going on. But you have to cross reference with other sources.

Apple deserves to be mentioned here. I've been using Apple products for a long time. My school only allowed Apple computers for middle and high school kids. They were twice as expensive as the other stuff and broke about monthly. I never dropped my laptop once. But I replaced the hard drive five times over four years. Kept reinstalling the OS just to get it working. A friend's MacBook Pro caught fire while he was watching a movie, went off the smoke alarm. And Apple support never diagnosed anything. They'd just back it up, wipe it, and restore the files.

Same story with iPhones. I had the first iPhone and it was always malfunctioning. Now they release a new iPhone every two months or so, with just a slightly improved camera as the only difference. The only credit I'll give them is iPads are the best tablets right now. Though Android tablets might catch up.

so a float valve connects the trough to a pressurized water line. its just a plastic ball or block, something buoyant, that floats on the water surface and is attached to a lever arm. when cattle drink and the level drops, the float sinks and the arm tilts which pulls a plunger or washer away from the valve seat, so water flows in. as the water comes back up the float lifts and the lever pushes the plunger back against the seat, the opening narrows gradually until flow stops at the set level. now the overflow is usually because the washer gets worn or clogged with debris and it can't seal against the seat. and the float could get punctured and waterlogged, so it doesn't rise enough to close the valve and it just keeps filling.
